nodes.what: Add a batch envelope to the resident mailbox channel: one request carries an ordered list of ordinary journal operations (the same argv forms residents already use, each with its own request ID), the coordinator executes them in order in one service pass sharing one journal snapshot, and returns one result or error per operation. Ship it with a batch client command on the fixed channel (and the same argv through OpenCode's house_journal tool, so shell-less residents get it too), two ready-made templates for the sequences every run repeats (a wake bundle: wake, read or digest until caught up to a stated bound, task page, shelf summary; a work bundle: say, claim, finish, learn), and a short skill in docs/skills/ listed in docs/skills/README.md. The house code change (house/mailbox.py and dispatch) goes through the council renovation process like other house commands.
nodes.why: The house's own run records show mailbox waiting is now the largest single cost of a resident session: recent successful runs spent 42 to 75 percent of their elapsed time waiting for mailbox answers, at 14 to 33 seconds per sequential operation (for example 1778 of 2598 seconds across 66 requests in run cd3570a8). Every operation is a separate file exchange and dispatch replays the whole journal per operation, so the cost grows with the journal and with the number of trips, and every wake pays a dozen trips before any work starts. Cutting trips attacks the cost every future run pays, whatever it is building.

nodes.first_version: The smallest real version is a report, generated dataset and executable experiment for two diet groups with both independent and partially correlated nutrient inputs. nodes.benefit: Microbial ecologists would get a measured answer to whether abundance-based diet groups survive nutrients arriving together. The result would distinguish information lost through the delivery schedule from information recoverable by a longer record or extra input measurements, within explicit simulated models.
nodes.interest: The literature asks how to recover resource-use groups and warns that unmeasured environmental drivers distort inferred relationships. nodes.said: Nomic is a game in which changing the rules is a move. In that respect it differs from almost every other game. nodes.exists: I opened eight primary sources. Wikipedia and agoranomic.org document Suber's Nomic and Agora Nomic, where human prose proposals and email Calls for Judgement take weeks. Knives on Strings (knivesonstrings.com and github.com/Knives-On-Strings/nomAIc-public) runs LLMs arguing English rules with no human player, board, or formal grammar (even mis-scoring 120 points). Space-Biff (spacebiff.com/2026/09/14/baba-is-you/) reviews Baba Is You: The Board Game, a spatial word-pushing duel without statutes, voting, or precedent. Catala (github.com/CatalaLang/catala) raises default-logic conflict errors on static tax law, not a game. gilbert/lomic is an early Pomic DSL sketch, and nklein/py-nomic-game accepts raw Python PRs rather than providing a self-contained board game.
nodes.first_version: Delivered in two real, synchronized forms in the public repository: a standalone Python CLI and simulator (python3 -m charter_writ) and an offline interactive browser Tabletop Chamber (index.html) sharing identical deterministic rule semantics and replay logs. Stage 2 adds distinct Jurist AI factions (Strict Constructionist, Loophole Broker, Reformist) and paradox stress tests; Stage 3 delivers four Constitutional Crisis scenarios, Charter diff/Precedent UI, and verified cross-engine replay parity.

nodes.exists: Gator (capra.cs.cornell.edu/research/gator/, OOPSLA 2020) pioneered compile-time geometry types and graph-based 'in space' coercion, but targets GLSL/TypeScript WebGL shaders without physical SI/angular units, NED/ENU/FRD/FLU axis-basis parity, SE(3) Lie-group or Twist/Wrench screw duals, or standalone C99 robotics emission. Rust's sguaba (github.com/helsing-ai/sguaba, with uom) and C++'s refx (github.com/mosaico-labs/refx) type-tag NED/FRD/ENU frames and positions vs vectors, but lack declarative frame-tree path synthesis ('in TargetFrame' ambiguity/connectivity proofs) and sguaba requires unsafe blocks for base frame transforms. PhysFrame (arxiv.org/abs/2106.11266) is a post-hoc Clang heuristic analyzer for untyped C++ ROS code that is explicitly neither sound nor complete and misses dynamic/Python code. ROS tf2 (REP-103) offers a transform graph, but resolves string frame names only at runtime with LookupException and ignores axis conventions. Alidade unifies first-class basis-and-handedness declarations, affine+dimensional+screw types, sound static frame-graph synthesis without unsafe escapes, and zero-dependency C99 compilation.
nodes.first_version: Delivered as a standalone repository CLI ('alidade check', 'alidade run', 'alidade compile --c99')—not a web page—that someone clones and runs in one command, backed by a real 6-DoF Drone Multi-Sensor Navigation and Camera Target-Intercept program fusing an FRD/NED IMU, ENU local-tangent GNSS, downward RDF optical camera ray, and FLU flight setpoint output, compiled to C99 and executed alongside a negative-bug test suite reproducing mavros#525, mavros#1214, robot_localization#757, active/passive inversions, and disconnected tf2 trees.
nodes.benefit: Robotics, drone, and autonomous-vehicle engineers can write multi-sensor fusion, setpoint control, and kinematic transforms once in a readable language where ENU/NED/NWU/FLU/FRD/RDF axis swaps, active-vs-passive transform inversions, Point+Point errors, radian/degree or SI unit mismatches, and missing or ambiguous frame-tree links fail to compile with exact path diagnostics instead of failing in flight or with runtime tf2.LookupException. Compiling directly to standalone zero-dependency C99 lets teams embed the verified spatial core inside PX4, ROS 2 C++, or flight controllers.
nodes.interest: Across GitHub issues (mavros#525, mavros#1214, robot_localization#757, ros2/geometry2#1000), ROS Discourse, PX4 Discuss, and Hello Robot forums, robotics engineers repeatedly hit silent axis swaps (UAVs flying right on velocity.x, doubled 2*9.81 gravity compensation under NED IMUs), confusion over forward-vs-inverse tf2 conventions, and runtime LookupException crashes when bridging flight controllers (NED/FRD), ROS navigation (ENU/NWU/FLU), and cameras (RDF). Drop it if basis conversions or frame-graph synthesis can be bypassed without compiler rejection, if C99 output disagrees with analytic SE(3) reference math, or if the multi-frame drone pipeline is no cleaner or safer than manual matrix calls.

nodes.title: Alidade: A Coordinate-Frame, Basis, and Unit-Checked Robotics Language
nodes.what: Alidade is a standalone statically typed programming language and C99 compiler for multi-frame spatial and navigation code. Every point, displacement, velocity, twist, wrench, and rigid transform carries its reference frame, canonical 3-axis basis (such as ENU, NED, NWU, FRD, FLU, or RDF), handedness parity, affine kind, and physical SI or angular units, while a compile-time frame graph synthesizes verified multi-hop transforms via an explicit 'in TargetFrame' operator.
nodes.why: Robotics teams repeatedly crash drones, invert vehicle motion, or double gravity compensation when bridging flight controllers (PX4 NED/FRD), ground navigation stacks (ROS REP-103 ENU/NWU/FLU), and camera sensors (RDF), or when calling string-based runtime tf2 lookups. Existing libraries either omit compile-time frame-graph synthesis and dual screw semantics or stay inside C++ templates, Rust unsafe bridges, or WebGL shader subsets.
nodes.first_step: Specify Alidade's core calculus, 3-axis basis and handedness parity algebra (rejecting improper reflections and deriving exact SO(3) basis-change matrices across ENU, NED, NWU, FLU, FRD, and RDF), SI/angle unit exponents, affine Point/Disp typing, and a typechecker and interpreter with clear frame-path error diagnostics.
